facts.claim: Prohibition took effect across the United States
facts.context: The Eighteenth Amendment and the Volstead Act banned the manufacture and sale of alcohol from January 1920.
facts.goDeeper: Drinking itself was never illegal. Buying, making and selling were.

facts.claim: Prohibition was repealed by the Twenty-first Amendment
facts.context: Ratified in December 1933, the only amendment ever passed to repeal another.
facts.goDeeper: Repeal was partly a revenue measure: the Depression had gutted federal income and liquor taxes were worth having back.

source.title: Twenty-first Amendment to the United States Constitution

facts.claim: The Nineteenth Amendment gave American women the vote
facts.context: Ratified in August 1920 after a campaign lasting more than seventy years.
facts.goDeeper: Tennessee ratified by a single vote, cast by a young legislator whose mother had written telling him to.

source.title: Nineteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution

facts.claim: The St Valentine's Day Massacre took place in Chicago
facts.context: Seven men were shot dead in a garage on 14 February 1929, in a killing widely attributed to Capone's organisation.
facts.goDeeper: Nobody was ever convicted. The public revulsion marked the beginning of the end for Capone.

facts.claim: Al Capone was convicted of tax evasion
facts.context: Sentenced to eleven years in October 1931, after prosecutors gave up on the violent crimes.
facts.goDeeper: He served part of it on Alcatraz, and was released in 1939 with his health ruined by untreated syphilis.

facts.claim: Charles Lindbergh flew alone and nonstop across the Atlantic
facts.context: He flew New York to Paris in May 1927, covering about 3,600 miles in 33 and a half hours.
facts.goDeeper: He carried no radio and no parachute, to save weight, and stayed awake the whole way.

facts.claim: The Jazz Singer brought synchronised speech to feature films
facts.context: Released October 1927, it ended the silent era within a few years.
facts.goDeeper: It contains only a few minutes of speech, much of it improvised by Al Jolson.

facts.claim: F. Scott Fitzgerald published The Great Gatsby
facts.context: It sold modestly and Fitzgerald died in 1940 believing himself a failure.
facts.goDeeper: Its revival came from free copies distributed to American troops during the Second World War.

facts.claim: The Wall Street crash ended the boom
facts.context: Prices collapsed over several days in late October 1929.
facts.goDeeper: The market did not regain its 1929 peak until 1954, a quarter of a century later.

facts.claim: Price of a Ford Model T by the mid-1920s
facts.context: The price fell to around $260, from over $800 when it launched in 1908.
facts.goDeeper: Ford cut the price as production volume rose, on the theory that his own workers should be able to buy one.

facts.claim: American households with a radio by 1930
facts.context: Around 40 percent had one by 1930, up from almost none at the start of the decade.
facts.goDeeper: Commercial broadcasting barely existed in 1920. By 1930 it was a national industry.

facts.claim: Estimated speakeasies operating in New York City at Prohibition's height
facts.context: Estimates ran from 20,000 to 100,000, none of them reliable for obvious reasons.
facts.goDeeper: The city had far more illegal bars under Prohibition than it had legal saloons before it.

facts.claim: Peak of the Dow Jones average before the 1929 crash
facts.context: It closed at 381.17 on 3 September 1929.
facts.goDeeper: By July 1932 it had fallen to 41, a decline of about 89 percent.

facts.claim: The Empire State Building opened in New York
facts.context: Completed in just over a year and opened in May 1931, at the start of the Depression.
facts.goDeeper: It stood largely empty for years and was nicknamed the Empty State Building.

facts.claim: The Harlem Renaissance flourished during the 1920s
facts.context: A concentration of Black literature, music and art centred on Harlem, with Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston and Duke Ellington among its figures.
facts.goDeeper: It was fed by the Great Migration, which brought some six million Black Americans north over several decades.

facts.claim: Drinking alcohol was itself a crime under Prohibition
facts.context: The Eighteenth Amendment banned manufacture, sale and transport. Consumption and private possession of alcohol bought beforehand were not offences.
facts.goDeeper: Wealthy households stocked cellars before the deadline and drank legally for years.

facts.claim: The flapper style was widely condemned at the time
facts.context: Short hair, raised hemlines, smoking and dancing in public drew heavy criticism from press and pulpit.
facts.goDeeper: The look is now shorthand for the decade, which rather obscures how transgressive it was meant to be.

facts.claim: Alcohol consumption fell during Prohibition
facts.context: Consumption dropped sharply at first and remained below pre-1920 levels for years, though it recovered from its low point.
facts.goDeeper: Deaths from cirrhosis fell too. The policy is usually remembered purely as a failure, which is not quite the whole picture.

facts.claim: A Tennessee teacher was prosecuted in 1925 for teaching evolution
facts.context: John Scopes was convicted and fined $100 in a trial that drew national radio coverage.
facts.goDeeper: The conviction was later overturned on a technicality, and the law itself stayed on the books until 1967.

facts.claim: Buying goods on instalment credit became widespread in the 1920s
facts.context: Cars, radios and appliances were increasingly bought on time payments, a new habit for most households.
facts.goDeeper: By 1929 a substantial share of consumer durables was bought on credit, which made the bust that followed considerably worse.
